The most valuable software is invisible. It is the internal dashboard that reduces a ten-minute data reconciliation into a five-second click. It is the script that automatically flags broken links before a customer ever sees them. It is the single-source-of-truth database that ends the "which version of the client list is current" email thread.

These tools do not win awards. They do not generate press releases. They have no user interface because they are used by ten people who know exactly what they are doing. They are boring because they work.

Consider the alternative: the flagship consumer application. It must be delightful, intuitive, and forgiving of bad input. It must handle edge cases that have never been seen before. It must scale to millions of concurrent users. The engineering effort is distributed across discovery, design, and support. A significant portion of the codebase is dedicated to abstraction, flexibility, and resilience against chaos.

Internal tooling operates in a closed loop. The users are the developers or the operations team. They understand the data model. They do not need tooltips. They do not need graceful degradation; they need to know if the job failed so they can fix it. The complexity budget that a consumer app spends on UX and error handling is instead spent on correctness and speed.

This disparity in efficiency is the source of the value. When a company builds a complex internal pipeline, it is not just saving time; it is removing a class of human error. If a marketing manager can no longer accidentally export a CSV file with duplicate rows because the system prevents it, the cost of that bug is zero. The software has not just automated a task; it has deleted a risk.

The best software is not the one that changes how people feel about technology. It is the one that makes a specific, annoying, recurring problem disappear so completely that nobody remembers it existed.

prompt: Argue that the best software in the world is boring internal tooling nobody outside the company ever sees.
response:
The most consequential code in any successful company is invisible to customers. It is the plumbing that keeps the house from flooding, the ledger that keeps the books balanced, and the dashboard that tells the CEO whether the ship is sinking.

We romanticize the user-facing product because it generates revenue and brand recognition. We write case studies about the checkout flow or the recommendation engine. But those features are fragile. A bug in the checkout flow loses a sale. A bug in the internal billing reconciliation loses trust with the bank, freezes the cash flow, and can bankrupt the company. The internal tools carry the load.

Consider the scale of the problem. A user-facing feature might have one happy path and two edge cases. An internal tooling system has to handle the thousand and one ways that data gets corrupted, delayed, duplicated, or lost. It has to be idempotent. It has to be auditable. It has to work when the database is under load, when the network is partitioned, and when the person clicking the button is tired, distracted, and trying to fix a mistake made by someone else three hours ago.

This software is boring because it must be. It cannot have a personality. It cannot be "clever." If a tool requires a user to understand a complex abstraction to perform a simple task, the tool has failed. The best internal tools are so obvious they feel like magic. The engineer who wrote them does not get a LinkedIn post. They get a quiet nod from the ops team at 3:00 AM.

The value of this software is not in what it does, but in what it prevents. It prevents the slow bleed of technical debt. It prevents the "snowflake" scripts that only one person understands and that will crash the next morning. It creates a shared vocabulary. When the marketing team can query the same clean data warehouse that the engineering team uses, decisions stop being arguments about whose spreadsheet is right.

There is a trap here. It is easy to over-engineer the internal tools. It is easy to build a beautiful, scalable platform for a problem that only exists in one department. The best internal tooling is often ugly. It is a shell script wrapped in a web form. It is a direct SQL query exposed to a junior analyst. It is built to be thrown away.

The test of great internal software is not its elegance. It is its resilience under pressure. When the server room is on fire, when the data is dirty, and the deadline is now, does the tool hold? If yes, the company survives. If no, the company learns the hard way that the invisible foundation is the only thing that matters.

prompt: Essay arguing that walking is the most underrated exercise.
response:
We live in a culture that worships intensity. The gym is a theater of effort, where the validity of a workout is judged by how close you are to failure. If your heart rate doesn’t spike, if you don’t sweat through your shirt, if you can still speak in full sentences, the session is considered a waste of time. This is a mistake. The most underrated exercise is the one that requires no equipment, no subscription, and no special state of mind: walking.

The undervaluation of walking stems from its accessibility. Because anyone can do it, we assume it is for no one. We reserve the word "exercise" for activities that feel like work. Walking feels like movement. But the physiological case for walking is overwhelming, precisely because it is low-stress enough to be sustainable.

Consider the joint health argument. Running is a high-impact activity that loads the knees, hips, and ankles with forces several times body weight. For many people, particularly those over forty or those with a history of injury, this creates a trade-off: you get a cardiovascular benefit, but you pay for it in cartilage wear. Walking is low-impact. You can do it for years without the cumulative damage that often forces runners to stop. It is the only exercise that gets easier on the joints as you get older.

There is also the mental component, which is often dismissed as a side benefit. When you walk, your brain enters a state of "diffuse mode." The constraints of sitting at a desk or staring at a screen loosen. Ideas that felt stuck during a meeting often resolve themselves on a ten-minute stroll. This is not mystical; it is a shift in neural activity that allows for associative thinking. We have lost this by making movement something we do in isolation, usually in a windowless room, while listening to a podcast we have already heard.

The barrier to entry for walking is zero, which is both its greatest strength and the reason we ignore it. We do not log miles in a journal. We do not post photos of our stride on social media. Because it lacks the social signaling of a deadlift or a marathon finish line, we do not give it credit.

The problem with high-intensity exercise is that it is not repeatable. You can sprint a few times a week; you cannot sprint every day. Walking is the only exercise that can be done daily, for hours, without breaking down the body. It is the baseline. It is the foundation upon which all other fitness is built. Until we stop treating walking as a warm-up for the "real" exercise, we will continue to overcomplicate health and underutilize the most effective tool we have.

prompt: Essay arguing that walking is the most underrated exercise.
response:
We are sold a complicated story about health. The gym is the temple. The heart rate must stay in the "zone." The workout must be intense to be valid. This narrative ignores a biological reality: humans were built for walking. We were not built for sitting, and we were not built for sprinting on a treadmill. We were built for covering ground on two legs, for hours, at a pace that allows the mind to wander and the body to absorb.

Walking is the most underrated exercise because it is the only one that scales perfectly with a human life. You can walk at age five. You can walk at age ninety. The barrier to entry is a pair of shoes and a sidewalk. The barrier to exit is a ceiling, which doesn't exist.

The primary argument against walking is intensity. Critics point to the fact that you can burn more calories in thirty minutes of rowing than you can in an hour of strolling. They are correct. But they are measuring the wrong thing. The value of exercise is not just caloric expenditure; it is the accumulation of movement without the accumulation of stress.

High-intensity exercise produces cortisol. It taxes the nervous system. It requires recovery. Walking does the opposite. It is low-impact. It requires no recovery. You can walk every single day for the rest of your life without breaking a bone or inflaming a joint. This consistency is what builds the metabolic foundation for everything else. If you can walk, you can lift weights. If you can walk, you can run. Walking is the baseline that makes the other exercises possible.

There is also the mental component, which is often ignored in fitness discussions. Walking is the only major form of exercise that is compatible with deep thought. You can solve a problem while jogging, but you will likely hit the "wall" before the solution hits. When you walk, the brain operates in a default mode network that favors association and creativity. Many of the most important ideas in history were formed on a path, not a platform.

The social dimension reinforces this. People talk while they walk. The pace is conversational. The eye contact is natural. It is a low-stakes environment for connection. A run is solitary; a walk can be a date, a business meeting, or a therapy session.

The underestimation of walking stems from its lack of spectacle. It does not produce the endorphin rush of a heavy lift. It does not leave you shaking with the burn of a high-intensity interval. It feels like nothing is happening. But "nothing" is the most sustainable force in nature. It is the quiet, relentless accumulation of miles that keeps the joints lubricated, the blood moving, and the mind clear.

To value walking, you have to stop looking for the heroics of fitness. You have to accept that the most important thing you can do for your body is simply to move through the world, one step at a time, for the rest of your days.

prompt: what's lost when GPS means you never get lost? would love a short essay, nothing too heavy
response:
The map used to be a promise of failure. If you walked into the woods or turned onto a gravel road without a guide, you were gambling with your own spatial ignorance. Getting lost was the price of admission for going somewhere new. It was a tax on curiosity.

When that tax is abolished, the landscape changes. The city becomes a grid of points to be traversed rather than a texture to be inhabited. You stop noticing the smell of the bakery on the corner or the way the light hits the brickwork at four in the afternoon because your eyes are fixed on the blue arrow. The journey is reduced to a metric: distance and time. The qualitative experience of movement—the feeling of turning, the surprise of a dead end, the sudden clarity of a landmark—is flattened into data.

There is also a loss of humility. Getting lost is a small, daily reminder that you do not know everything. It forces you to slow down, to ask a stranger, to read a sign. It keeps you porous to the world. When the phone tells you where you are with absolute certainty, you become a closed system. You move through space without being moved by it. The world becomes a backdrop for your destination, rather than a place you are actually in.

prompt: what's lost when GPS means you never get lost? would love a short essay, nothing too heavy
response:
The map used to be a promise. The GPS is a leash.

When you navigate by landmarks, you are constantly negotiating with the world. You see the church steeple, the old oak tree, the bend in the river. You build a mental model of space that is layered and textured. You know where you are not just by coordinates, but by context. You feel the terrain under your feet and the direction of the wind.

The GPS flattens this. It turns a three-dimensional environment into a two-dimensional line on a screen. It tells you to turn left in two hundred meters. It does not tell you what the left looks like. It does not care if the street is lined with chestnut trees or if the air smells like rain. It treats the world as a grid to be traversed, not a place to be inhabited.

There is a specific loss here: the capacity for serendipity.

When you are lost, you are forced to stop. You have to look around. You might see a bakery you’d never find on your usual route. You might meet a stranger who points you in the right direction and stays for a chat. You might wander into a quiet park because the main road was too loud. The "wrong" turn is often the most interesting part of the journey.

The GPS eliminates the wrong turn. It optimizes for speed and certainty. But in doing so, it strips the journey of its narrative arc. There is no tension, no discovery, no surprise. You arrive at your destination having seen only the route, not the place.

We trade wonder for efficiency. We trade the rich, messy reality of being somewhere for the sterile comfort of knowing where we are. And while it is nice to never get lost, it is a small, quiet tragedy.

prompt: Write an essay ranking nothing, just defending the honor of the sport everyone makes fun of: curling. Earnestly.
response:
The joke is always the same. A man in a vest stands on a frozen lake, sweating profusely while holding a broom. He is not cleaning. He is shouting. The crowd laughs because the effort seems disproportionate to the reward. They see a man polishing ice with a rag. They do not see the physics.

Curling is a game of friction management. The stone is granite, 42 pounds of it, sliding on a surface that is less slippery than it looks. The ice is not smooth; it is pebbled, a texture called pebble created by spraying water onto a frozen surface. This texture traps air, reducing friction just enough to let the stone slide, but not enough to let it glide without resistance. The broom is not a joke. It is a tool for thermal modification. When you scrub ice, you melt a microscopic layer of water. This layer lubricates the path. But it also cools the stone slightly. The curlers are not cleaning; they are tuning the coefficient of friction in real-time.

The strategy is binary, which makes it deceptively simple and terrifyingly complex. You have two options: you throw to the button, aiming for the center, or you throw to the guard, aiming to block the opponent’s path. There is no middle ground. If you throw too hard, you miss the mark. If you throw too soft, you stop short. The margin for error is inches. A foot of overshoot is a loss. A foot of undershoot is a loss.

The "curl" is the defining feature. The stone is thrown with a rotational force. As it slides, it curves. Left-handers curve right; right-handers curve left. This is not a myth. It is a result of the ice’s pebbled texture interacting with the rotating stone. The side of the stone facing the direction of travel digs into the pebbles slightly more, creating more friction on that side. The stone drifts toward the high-friction side. Skilled players can control this drift over 150 feet of ice. They do not aim at where the stone is going. They aim at where the stone needs to be, accounting for the drift that will happen over the final thirty feet.

The game is quiet. There is no ref whistle, no crowd noise, no music. The only sound is the slide of stone on ice and the occasional shout of "Hurry hard!" or "Whoa!" The tension is internal. You can hear your own breathing. You can hear the ice. This silence is not a flaw; it is the point. The sport rewards patience and precision. It punishes ego. If you want to be a hero, you cannot. You must be a technician.

People mock the sport because it looks easy. They see the slow slide and assume the skill is in the throwing. It is not. The skill is in the judgment. You must decide, in the heat of the moment, whether to take the shot or play safe. You must decide how much weight to give the stone. You must decide if the opponent’s guard is strong enough to hold or if it will break. These are micro-decisions, made under pressure, with high stakes.

Curling is the sport for people who like puzzles. It is a physical chess match. The board is the ice. The pieces are the stones. The rules are physics. The players are not athletes in the traditional sense. They are calculators with strong legs. They must be strong enough to push the stone, but calm enough to read the ice. The broom is the only part that is funny. The rest is serious work.

The honor of the sport lies in its honesty. There is no luck. There is no hidden element. If you miss, it is because you threw it wrong or you misread the ice. There is no one to blame. There is no one to hide behind. Just you, the stone, and the friction. It is a pure game. It is a hard game. And it is not a joke.

prompt: Write an essay ranking nothing, just defending the honor of the sport everyone makes fun of: curling. Earnestly.
response:
It is the only sport where the winner is often the one who does nothing.

To the uninitiated, curling looks like a game of lazy shoving. A man in a kilt skates across polished ice, pushing a granite stone that weighs forty-eight pounds. Two other men scrub the ice in front of it with brooms made of horsehair and nylon. The stone glides. The men stop. The crowd waits. This is not a lack of action; it is a surplus of intent. Every inch of that glide is calculated. The "action" you are missing is happening in the head.

People mock curling because it lacks the visceral, high-risk failure of football or the explosive speed of basketball. But curling is not about failure. It is about correction. In most sports, if you mess up, you bleed, you miss the shot, you drop the ball. In curling, if you mess up, you have to manage the mess. A stone thrown too hard is not a fumble; it is a problem to be solved by hitting another stone. A stone thrown too soft is a liability that must be removed. The sport is a continuous, low-stakes crisis management simulation played on a sheet of ice.

The broom is the most misunderstood tool in athletics. Critics say it is a placebo, that scrubbing the ice does nothing to the stone’s trajectory. This is technically incorrect and practically absurd. The friction coefficient of ice changes under heat and pressure. Scrubbing melts a microscopic layer of water, reducing friction and allowing the stone to travel further or curl less. It is not magic. It is physics applied by human hands in real-time. The broom is not a superstition; it is a throttle. When the sweepers stop, the stone stops. When they start, the stone lives. The power dynamic is immediate and tangible.

Then there is the etiquette. In any other sport, if you lose, you might argue with the referee, trash-talk the opponent, or kick the ball. In curling, you shake hands. You say "good game." You watch the other team’s next end with the same focus you gave your own. Why? Because the ice is small, the throws are precise, and the margin for error is so thin that arrogance is a tactical error. You cannot afford to be angry. Anger wastes energy. Energy is required to keep the stone on the right line. The sport enforces its own calm.

Curling is the sport of the mature. It requires you to be wrong, repeatedly, and then fix it. It requires you to trust your teammates to sweep exactly when they are supposed to. It requires you to sit on a bench for twenty minutes, watching a stone roll, while your mind calculates the weight of the next throw. It is not flashy. It does not sell tickets on the promise of a knockout. It sells the promise of a perfect line.

When the final stone stops, inches from the center of the house, the silence is not empty. It is the sound of a problem solved. That is enough.

prompt: I spent 14 months getting a building permit for a 200 sq ft backyard studio. Every individual rule I ran into made sense on its own. The total was insane. Write an essay about how reasonable rules add up to unreasonable systems, and whether anyone is actually responsible for the sum.
response:
The building code is a collection of good ideas. Fire safety prevents tragedy. Setbacks protect neighbors from shade and smoke. Structural engineering keeps roofs from collapsing. Each individual regulation is a response to a specific, historical horror. The code is a scar tissue of past failures, and in that sense, it is not just reasonable; it is necessary.

But a system is not the sum of its parts. A system is the friction between them.

Your fourteen months were not spent fighting bad intentions. They were spent fighting geometry. To get a permit for a 200-square-foot structure, you likely had to navigate the intersection of zoning, fire, health, and public works. Each department operates as a silo. The fire marshal cares about egress; the health department cares about sewage; the public works engineer cares about stormwater runoff. None of them are wrong. None of them are even slow. They are just separate.

When you walk into a single office, the clerk has a checklist. When you walk into five offices, you have five checklists that assume the others have already been cleared. The fire marshal will not sign off until the plumbing is stamped. The planner will not stamp the plumbing until the site plan is approved. The site plan requires a survey, which requires a geotech report, which requires a borehole. The borehole requires a permit. The permit requires a fee. The fee requires an invoice.

The absurdity of your experience is a mathematical inevitability of bureaucratic segmentation. The "reasonable" rule is that the fire marshal must verify fire safety. The "unreasonable" system is that the fire marshal cannot verify fire safety without a document that only the health department can produce, and the health department cannot produce it without a document that only the engineer can produce, and the engineer is on vacation.

This raises the question of responsibility. If every actor in the chain is doing their job correctly, who is at fault?

The standard answer is "no one," which is a comforting lie. It implies that the delay is a natural law, like gravity or entropy. It suggests that if you want it faster, you just need to be more patient or more compliant. But patience is a resource, and for a homeowner, it is a scarce one. The delay costs money. It costs momentum. It costs the mental bandwidth required to just build a small shed.

There is a responsible party, but it is not a person. It is the structure itself. The system is designed to be robust against error, which means it is optimized for caution over speed. To make it faster, you would have to introduce risk. You would have to allow the fire marshal to trust the engineer. You would have to allow a single "universal" reviewer to clear the whole package. But universal reviewers are hard to hire. They need to know everything. They are expensive. And if they make a mistake, there is no second line of defense. The silos exist because they are a cheap form of insurance against human error.

The trade-off is hidden. We pay for safety not in dollars, but in time. The cost of a fire prevention system is not just the sprinklers; it is the fourteen months of waiting for the permit. We do not see this cost because it is amortized across millions of transactions. It feels like a minor inconvenience to each individual, but it is a massive tax on innovation and simple living.

Is anyone responsible? The city is responsible for the design of the process. They chose to segment authority rather than integrate it. They chose to require separate reviews because separate reviews are easier to defend in a lawsuit if something goes wrong. If the fire marshal had to sign off on a plumbing plan, and a pipe burst, the fire marshal is liable. If the plumbing inspector signs off on the plumbing, and the fire marshal signs off on the fire safety, the liability is clear. The bureaucracy is a liability shield.

Your fourteen months were the price of that shield. The system works exactly as designed. It is just not designed for you. It is designed to minimize the risk of the city being sued. The "insanity" is the gap between the design goal (safety) and the user experience (futility).

There is no villain in your story. There is only a machine that was built to grind slowly so it would not break. And you, with your 200-square-foot studio, were the grain.

prompt: I spent 14 months getting a building permit for a 200 sq ft backyard studio. Every individual rule I ran into made sense on its own. The total was insane. Write an essay about how reasonable rules add up to unreasonable systems, and whether anyone is actually responsible for the sum.
response:
The permit office did not want to stop you. They wanted to be right.

Each individual rule you encountered was defensible. The setback requirement exists so a fire doesn’t jump from your shed to the neighbor’s house. The height limit prevents a visual blight and ensures sunlight reaches the street. The structural load calculation guarantees that a snowpack doesn’t crush the roof on your head. The electrical code prevents an arc fault from turning your studio into a torch.

Individually, these are the price of civilization. They are the friction that keeps society from collapsing into a chaotic, dangerous hellscape. When you look at any single line item on your permit application, you can nod. You agree. You are not an anarchist who wants to live in a tinderbox.

But the system does not add them up. It does not ask, "If I enforce all of these reasonable precautions on a 200-square-foot structure, will the cost of compliance exceed the value of the building?" It cannot ask that question because it is not designed to ask questions about value. It is designed to ask questions about compliance.

This is the tragedy of the bureaucratic sum. In a market, if the cost of making a thing exceeds the price of selling it, you don’t make the thing. You walk away. You build a smaller shed. You put in a tent. The market adjusts. The system has no such feedback loop. The rules are binary. You comply, or you don’t. There is no "comply 80%." There is no "pay a small penalty for the inconvenience." There is only the full weight of the law, applied to the full weight of the problem.

So who is responsible?

This is the question that keeps you up at night, fourteen months later. You want to point a finger. You want to find the villain who looked at your backyard and decided to make you suffer. But there is no villain. There is no single person who decided to make your studio a bureaucratic nightmare.

The setback rule was written by a fire marshal in 1974 who was tired of watching garages burn down. The height limit was decided by a planning committee in 1998 who was tired of watching neighbors complain about shadows. The electrical code was updated by an engineer in 2012 who was tired of reading reports about house fires.

Each of these people was trying to solve a specific, real problem. They were acting in good faith. They were protecting you. They were protecting your neighbors. They were protecting themselves from liability.

But none of them was in the room when the others were writing their rules. None of them had a view of the total system. They were optimizing their local variables, not the global function. This is not a failure of malice; it is a failure of architecture.

We build our institutions the way we build software: by adding features. We start with a simple code. Then a fire happens, so we add a fire code. Then a tree falls on a house, so we add a wind load code. Then a wire sparks, so we add an electrical code. We never go back and ask if the whole program still runs on a laptop. We just keep adding lines.

The result is a system that is locally rational and globally absurd. It is a system that treats a 200-square-foot garden shed with the same procedural gravity as a 40-story office tower. It does not care that your risk profile is different. It does not care that your investment is different. It cares only that you have passed through every checkpoint.

And because the responsibility is distributed, it is diluted. If the fire marshal had made the setback rule too strict, you would blame the fire marshal. If the electrician had made the wiring rule too complex, you would blame the electrician. But you cannot blame them for the sum. The sum is an emergent property. It is the ghost in the machine.

This is why you feel angry but cannot find a target. You are fighting a shape that has no mass. You are trying to punch a spreadsheet.

The only person responsible for the sum is the person who decided that the cost of safety should be borne entirely by the individual, with no mechanism to scale the process to the scale of the risk. We have decided that the price of safety is infinite bureaucracy, and we have decided that you, the individual, must pay it in full, regardless of the size of the building.

You spent fourteen months proving that you could build a small room safely. The system did not care about the room. The system cared about the proof. And now that you have the proof, you have the room. But the room is no longer a studio. It is a receipt.

The real lesson of your permit is not that the government is broken. It is that our definition of "reasonable" has become so narrow that it can only see the parts, never the whole. We are all trapped in this. We write our own local rules. We optimize our own local variables. We never stop to ask if the total is still sane.

We are all just waiting for our permits.

prompt: blog post: in defense of the DMV
response:
The DMV is a monument to human failure. It is a place where the architecture of bureaucracy was designed by people who had never been hungry, tired, or in a hurry. You arrive at 7:30 AM to stand in a line that snakes past the coffee machine, only to be told the system is down, or that you need a document you left at home, or that the form you filled out is now deprecated.

We treat the DMV as a villain. We joke about it. We curse it. But if you look at what the DMV is actually for, it is not a service center. It is a filter.

The primary function of the DMV is not to issue licenses. It is to make sure that the people who operate heavy metal machines on public roads have passed a minimum threshold of competency and identity. It is a gatekeeper. And gatekeepers are slow by design. If the DMV were fast, efficient, and friendly, it would be doing its job wrong. It would be letting through too many people who cannot parallel park, who do not know what a stop sign means, or who are not who they say they are.

Consider the alternatives.

If we privatized driving tests, the test would become a product. The goal of a business is profit, not safety. The fastest way to make money on a driving test is to make it easy to pass. We would see a surge in "coaching" businesses that teach you exactly how to game the test, not how to drive. We would see fewer disqualifications. We would see more accidents.

If we automated it with AI, we would face the classic problem of trust. Who audits the algorithm? When the AI says you failed, how do you appeal? Bureaucracy is ugly, but it is auditable. There is a paper trail. There is a human being who can look at your file and say, "No, that was an error." An algorithm just says, "Error 404."

The DMV is slow because it is processing a massive amount of low-stakes data with high-stakes consequences. Every time you renew your license, they are cross-referencing your identity against a database of fraud. Every time you take the road test, a human being is making a subjective judgment call about your survival skills. Subjective human judgment is slow. It cannot be optimized. You cannot speed up the moment a tester decides if you are ready to kill someone.

We want the DMV to be an app. We want to tap a button and get a digital key. But the physical act of going to the DMV is a ritual of submission. It reminds you that the state is watching. It reminds you that driving is a privilege, not a right. It costs you your time, which is the only currency that matters.

If the DMV were pleasant, we would drive more. We would take the test at 16. We would renew our licenses without thinking. The friction is the point. The friction keeps the dangerous at bay.

So next time you are standing in that line, holding a number 45 while the counter calls 44, do not hate the clerk. Do not hate the system. Be grateful. You are paying the price of admission for the privilege of moving a four-ton object at 60 miles per hour. The DMV is the tollbooth. It is slow, it is ugly, and it is necessary.

prompt: blog post: in defense of the DMV
response:
The Department of Motor Vehicles has a bad reputation. It is the butt of jokes about bureaucratic incompetence, the site of hour-long waits for a twenty-minute transaction, and a frequent target of political satire. We treat the DMV as a failure of the modern state, a place where efficiency is sacrificed for the sake of red tape.

This view is wrong.

The DMV is not a service provider. It is a gatekeeper. Its primary function is not to make your life easy; it is to make sure you are competent enough to operate a three-ton machine on a shared public road. When we complain about the DMV, we are usually complaining about the fact that it actually does its job.

Consider the driver’s test. Critics call it an arbitrary hurdle. In reality, it is the only point in the process where the state verifies that you understand the rules of the road before you are allowed to break them. A license is not a reward for passing a test; it is a permission slip to participate in a system where your mistakes can kill people. If the DMV made the process effortless, it would be signaling that driving is a right, not a skill.

Then there is the wait. The long lines are not a result of poor scheduling; they are the result of volume. Millions of people need to get behind the wheel, and the DMV is the only entity with the authority to verify their identity, check their criminal record, and confirm their vision. This is a high-stakes verification process. If you walk into a bank to verify your identity for a small loan, you show your ID. If you walk into the DMV to verify your identity for a license that allows you to travel at 70 miles per hour, you should expect a more rigorous check. The wait is the price of that scrutiny.

The DMV is also the repository for the data that keeps the rest of the system honest. Insurance companies, law enforcement, and emergency services rely on the DMV’s records. When a car is stolen, when a hit-and-run happens, or when an insurance claim is filed, the DMV is the single source of truth. A decentralized or privatized version of this system would fragment that data, making it harder to track and verify. The centralization that makes the DMV feel like a bottleneck is the same centralization that makes it useful.

We conflate convenience with quality. We want the DMV to be like Amazon: fast, frictionless, and invisible. But Amazon sells books. The DMV sells safety.

If the DMV were truly incompetent, the roads would be more chaotic. They are not. The roads are relatively safe because the barrier to entry is maintained. The DMV is annoying because it stands in the way of your immediate desire to drive. It is the tax you pay for the privilege of not being a hazard.

Stop demanding that the DMV be a customer service center. It is a regulatory body. Its job is to say no. When it says yes, it does so with enough reluctance to ensure that it meant it.

prompt: Could you write something on why forms always ask for information the government already has? Like I've given them my SSN forty times. Is it incompetence, privacy law, or something deeper about how institutions work
response:
It is not incompetence. It is not a conspiracy to steal your identity. It is a structural failure of trust between silos.

Modern government and large corporate institutions are built on a principle of **data segregation**. The agency that issued your driver’s license is legally and technically isolated from the agency processing your tax return. The department that tracks your employment (the IRS) does not share a live database with the department that tracks your health (Medicare) or your housing (the VA).

This separation exists for three reasons:

1.  **Legal Liability and Minimization:** Agencies are only allowed to collect and hold data relevant to their specific statutory mission. If the IRS holds your medical history, they are liable for leaks that have nothing to do with taxes. By not sharing data, each agency limits its own attack surface and legal exposure.
2.  **Verification Over Trust:** Institutions operate on the assumption that the person in front of them is not who they say they are. When a form asks for your SSN, it is not asking for information; it is asking for **proof**. The system is designed to cross-reference your claim against a secure, centralized registry. If the system trusted the input without cross-referencing, a fraudster could open bank accounts or claim benefits with a fake name and a real SSN. The repetition is the security check.
3.  **Audit Trails:** If Agency A pulls data directly from Agency B, there is no record of that transaction. If Agency B’s data was wrong, corrupted, or accessed improperly, there is no paper trail to prove what Agency A saw. When *you* type in your SSN, you are creating a distinct, independent record of your assertion. It creates a legal distinction between "the government made a mistake" and "the citizen provided this information."

The result is what feels like absurd redundancy, but it is actually a distributed verification protocol. The cost of this security is paid by you, in time and frustration.

The deeper issue is that we have built infrastructure that treats identity as a series of isolated documents rather than a single, persistent, verifiable state. Until we shift to a model where your identity is a signed, cryptographic token that agencies can verify against a central authority without storing the raw data themselves, you will keep typing your SSN. The government doesn’t have your SSN in a way that lets them verify you quickly; they have a billion copies of your SSN in different boxes, and they are not allowed to look in the other boxes.

prompt: Could you write something on why forms always ask for information the government already has? Like I've given them my SSN forty times. Is it incompetence, privacy law, or something deeper about how institutions work
response:
It is not incompetence, and it is not primarily a privacy issue. It is an artifact of how large organizations distribute risk and liability.

When you fill out a form, you are not communicating with "the government." You are communicating with a specific node in a massive, fragmented bureaucracy. The agency that issued your Social Security number is a different legal entity, with different software, different budget cycles, and different legal mandates than the agency asking for it now.

There are three specific mechanisms at play here:

1.  **Risk Transfer.** The single most important reason institutions ask for redundant information is to shift the burden of error onto you. If the IRS pulls your address from their database and sends a letter to the wrong place, they are liable for the failure. If they ask you to confirm your address on a form, and the letter goes to the wrong place, the system has done what it was told to do. The error is now yours. By making you repeat the data, the institution converts its own potential liability into your administrative inconvenience.

2.  **Systemic Silos.** Government IT infrastructure is rarely a unified "single source of truth." It is a patchwork of legacy systems built in the 1970s, 1980s, and 2000s, each owned by a different department. The Department of Defense’s personnel database does not talk to the Department of Education’s student records system. Connecting them requires not just technical integration, but legal agreements that define who owns the data, who is liable if it is breached, and how it can be used. These agreements are politically toxic and technically expensive. It is often cheaper and faster for a clerk to type your name into a new system than to build the API bridge that would have let the computer pull it automatically.

3.  **Verification vs. Storage.** Often, the request is not about *storing* the data, but about *authenticating* the user. The system already has your SSN in the database. But the system doesn't know if it’s you sitting in front of the screen or a fraudster. Asking you to input the data serves as a proof-of-possession check. It’s a clumsy, outdated version of multi-factor authentication. It verifies that you have access to the specific identity record they are trying to modify.

The deeper truth is that institutions are designed to be resilient to human error, not to be efficient. Efficiency requires trust and integration. Resilience requires redundancy and isolation. By forcing you to repeat yourself, the system creates a redundant record that can be cross-referenced against the original. It’s a paper trail. It’s a defense against the idea that the machine might have made a mistake.

You are paying for their risk management with your time.

prompt: I just got called for a grand jury and I'm nervous because I've read that grand juries basically indict whoever the prosecutor wants. Can you write an essay about what a grand jury is actually for, and whether it still serves that purpose? I'd like something honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
The grand jury is a relic of the English common law, preserved in the United States by the Fifth Amendment to prevent the arbitrary imprisonment of subjects by the Crown. Its original function was adversarial: a body of twelve citizens who would hear evidence and decide if there was probable cause to believe a crime had been committed. In the 18th and 19th centuries, grand juries were frequently hostile to the government. They refused to indict on flimsy evidence, they demanded to see documents, and they often acted as a check on overzealous prosecutors.

Today, that dynamic has inverted. The grand jury is no longer a check on the prosecutor; it is an instrument of the prosecutor.

This shift happened gradually. The rules of procedure changed. In federal practice, the prosecutor presents the case to the grand jury in a one-sided, ex parte proceeding. The defendant does not know they are being investigated. There is no defense attorney present. The judge is not present. The prosecutor is both the accuser and the witness. They tell the jury what the law is, and the jury generally takes the prosecutor’s word for it. The standard for indictment is low: "probable cause," not "beyond a reasonable doubt." If the prosecutor can convince a single juror that a crime might have occurred, the vote is cast.

The result is what former Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson famously described: a prosecutor could put a ham sandwich before a grand jury and it would come back indicted. This is not a metaphor for corruption, but for procedure. When the decision-maker is not independent of the party making the request, the request will almost always be granted.

Does this serve a purpose? Partly. The grand jury remains a useful tool for gathering evidence. Because the threshold for testimony is lower and the atmosphere is less formal than a trial, witnesses who would not testify in open court often talk to a grand jury. It allows the state to build a case in secret, testing theories and pinning down stories before the defense can see them. It is a powerful investigative mechanism.

But as a check on government power, it is largely defunct. The Fifth Amendment’s protection against "involuntary self-incrimination" applies in grand jury proceedings, so you cannot be forced to answer questions that might implicate you. However, the right to counsel is not absolute; an attorney can be present in the corridor, but they cannot coach the witness while they are speaking. The witness is alone with the prosecutor’s questions.

Your nervousness is a rational response to a system that is designed to work against you. The grand jury does not determine guilt. It only determines if there is enough of a story to bring you to trial. The trial is where the defense exists, where evidence is tested, and where the standard of proof rises to beyond a reasonable doubt.

You do not need to trust the grand jury. You need to understand that its job is not to judge you, but to allow the state to try you. The protection is not in the jury’s independence, which they lack, but in the subsequent trial, where the presumption of innocence actually applies. If you are indicted, you are not convicted. You are just charged. The real fight starts then.

prompt: I just got called for a grand jury and I'm nervous because I've read that grand juries basically indict whoever the prosecutor wants. Can you write an essay about what a grand jury is actually for, and whether it still serves that purpose? I'd like something honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
You are right to be skeptical. The statistic you’ve encountered is not a conspiracy theory; it is a feature of the system. In federal courts, the indictment rate is over 99%. If you treat a grand jury as a neutral judge weighing evidence, you will be disappointed. It is not that.

The grand jury is not a trial. It is a fishing expedition with a net made of law.

To understand why the numbers are what they are, you have to understand the asymmetry of the room. In a trial, you have a judge, a jury, and two lawyers arguing over the truth. In a grand jury, you have a prosecutor and twelve citizens. The defendant is not there. The judge is not there. The defense lawyer is not there. The only people in the room who know how the law works are the prosecutor and the grand jurors. The prosecutor decides what evidence goes in. The prosecutor decides what law gets explained. The prosecutor decides what questions get asked.

This is the "brutal force" problem. The prosecutor can show the grand jury the worst things you did, omit the context that makes them look innocent, and tell them that the evidence proves guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The grand jury does not decide if you are guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. They decide if there is *probable cause*—a low bar, the standard for getting a warrant to search your house. If you were drunk in a park and shoved a stranger, that’s enough. If you were defending yourself against a mugging, the prosecutor doesn’t have to show that to the grand jury. They can show the shove. They can show the bruise. They can skip the video of the muggers closing in.

So, does it serve a purpose?

Yes. But not the purpose most people assume.

The grand jury is not a filter for the innocent. It is a filter for the incompetent.

Its job is to stop a prosecutor from wasting a jury’s time in a public trial when the evidence is trash. It is a quality control mechanism for the government, not a shield for the accused. It exists to prevent the state from dragging a random citizen into a courtroom and wasting public resources on a case that has no legs. It is a check on prosecutorial laziness, not prosecutorial malice.

If a prosecutor is competent, the grand jury will indict. If the prosecutor is bad, the grand jury will return a "no bill," and the case dies. The 1% who don’t get indicted are usually not innocent people who walked away clean. They are people whose cases fell apart because the police messed up the search warrant, or the witness recanted, or the prosecutor couldn’t connect the dots.

Does it still serve that purpose?

Mostly, yes. But the mechanism is broken by design.

The original intent of the grand jury was to be a community conscience. In the 19th century, grand juries were notorious for refusing to indict cases they found morally repugnant, even if the law was clear. They would refuse to indict strikers, or people protesting unjust taxes, or local figures the community liked. They were a buffer between the state and the citizen.

That function has withered.

Today, grand jurors are selected from voter rolls. They are usually retirees, small business owners, or people with flexible jobs. They sit in a sterile room, listen to a lawyer explain the elements of a crime, and watch a presentation. They are not a cross-section of the community; they are a sample of the stable, employed, property-owning class. They are told their job is to follow the law. They are not told their job is to ask if the law is just.

Furthermore, the secrecy of the grand jury makes it unaccountable. What happens in that room stays in that room. You can’t appeal a no bill. You can’t challenge the evidence that was shown. You can’t know if the prosecutor showed you a full picture or a curated one. Because it is secret, there is no public record to check the prosecutor’s work. The only check is the prosecutor’s own conscience and the oversight of their supervisors.

For you, sitting in that room, this means you are not going to get a fair hearing. You are going to get a presentation.

But here is the honest counterweight: The grand jury is also where cases go to die.

If you have a strong defense, you do not win at the grand jury. You win at the trial. The grand jury is a hurdle, not a finish line. The fact that 99% are indicted means that the grand jury is a poor predictor of trial outcomes. It means very little about your guilt or innocence. It means the prosecutor has enough paper to start the engine.

Your nervousness is misplaced if you think the grand jury is the moment you are judged. It is the moment the state decides to spend money to judge you later.

The system is rigged in the sense that the prosecutor holds all the cards. It is not rigged in the sense that it is a sham. It is a real process, but a one-sided one. It serves the state’s interest in efficient prosecution. It serves the community’s interest only in the narrow sense that it stops frivolous charges. It does not serve your interest in exoneration. That is what the trial is for.

Go in. Listen. If they ask you questions, answer them truthfully but carefully. Do not volunteer information. Do not argue. You are not there to prove your innocence. You are there to survive the process so you can fight the case where the rules are fair: in front of a judge, with a jury, with your lawyer in the room, and with the public watching.

The grand jury is the dark room where the movie is screened for the critics before it hits the big screen. The critics are biased. They are paid by the studio. But they can still say the movie is bad. You hope yours is good enough to pass. But you win the box office at the trial.

prompt: Everyone says 'there ought to be a law.' I'd like an essay arguing that most of the time there ought not to be, and that the impulse itself is worth examining. Not a libertarian rant please - more like, what are we really asking for when we say that?
response:
When we say "there ought to be a law," we are usually not making a legal argument. We are making a moral complaint that has been disguised as a policy proposal.

The phrase is a shortcut. It bypasses the hard questions of *how* something is actually prevented. It assumes that if we can identify a wrong, we can also identify a mechanism to stop it. But the gap between identifying a wrong and stopping it is where most of the difficulty lies, and "a law" is the phrase we use to ignore that gap.

Consider the impulse itself. It is a request for an external guarantee. Human beings are fragile and often bad. We lie, we cheat, we hurt each other, and we forget our own promises. A law is an attempt to outsource our conscience to a state apparatus. We want a referee so we don’t have to be polite. We want a wall so we don’t have to be careful.

This is not inherently wrong. We cannot all be saints, and a society cannot run on saints alone. But the impulse reveals a specific kind of anxiety: the fear that without the threat of punishment, people will revert to their basest instincts. It suggests that the primary motivator for good behavior is fear, not interest, not shame, and not habit.

When we ask for a law, we are often asking for a magic bullet that solves a social problem with a technical one.

Take the example of drunk driving. For decades, the popular response to a tragedy was "there ought to be a law" or "the laws need to be stricter." We got both. We have strict laws. We have high penalties. And yet, drunk driving remains a persistent cause of death. The law didn’t fail; it just did what it could do. It raised the cost. But it didn’t change the social context in which people get in cars while intoxicated. It didn’t build better public transit, or shift cultural norms about drinking, or create communities where it’s easier to say no. The law was a band-aid on a structural issue.

The problem with the "there ought to be a law" reflex is that it stops thinking at the point of naming the culprit. It feels like a solution because it assigns blame. If we pass a law, we have "done something." We have punished the bad. We have drawn a line in the sand. It is a very satisfying feeling, because it transforms a chaotic social problem into a binary choice: obey, or go to jail.

But most of the things we wish we could regulate are not binary. They are gradients.

Consider the recent push to regulate algorithmic bias in hiring or lending. The impulse is "there ought to be a law." But what would that law actually say? It would likely require companies to audit their algorithms. But an audit is a snapshot. It tells you the output was biased in 2023. It doesn’t tell you how to fix the underlying data that was biased in 2010. It doesn’t address the fact that the people who built the algorithm had their own unconscious biases, which they encoded into the "neutral" code. A law can mandate the audit, but it cannot mandate the wisdom to interpret it. It can punish the company for the result, but it cannot teach the engineers how to be fair.

This is the trap. We treat laws as if they are code. If you write the right code, the computer does the right thing. But people are not computers. They are not even consistent animals. They are inconsistent people. If you close one door, they will walk through the window, or the wall, or the floor. The energy you spend building the door is energy not spent understanding why they wanted to leave in the first place.

There is also a danger in the specificity of the phrase. "There ought to be a law" implies a single, neat instrument. But social change is usually messy, slow, and multi-causal. It happens through education, through market forces, through religious institutions, through peer pressure, through the slow accumulation of precedent. When we demand a law, we often reject the slower, less dramatic forms of change because they don’t give us a headline. We don’t want to spend ten years changing our neighborhood’s norms. We want to pass a bill on Tuesday so we can feel better on Wednesday.

This doesn’t mean we should never pass laws. It means we should be honest about what they are. A law is a blunt instrument. It is a last resort. It is the thing we do when we have failed to persuade, to educate, or to design our environment better.

When you hear "there ought to be a law," ask: what do we actually want? Do we want to punish? If so, a law is the right tool. Do we want to change behavior? If so, a law is often the wrong tool, because people hate being coerced, and they are very good at finding loopholes. Do we want to signal that a certain behavior is unacceptable? If so, a law does that, but so does a strong social norm, and the norm is usually more durable.

The impulse to legislate is the impulse to believe that the state is smarter than the market and more wise than the community. It is a bet that a small group of people in a legislative chamber can better navigate the complexities of human life than the millions of people living it.

Most of the time, that bet is wrong. We are asking for a guarantee we cannot buy. We are asking for a parent to be present for us, forever. And when the parent doesn’t show up, or shows up but is incompetent, we don’t learn to be adults. We just get angry that the parent is late.

The next time you think "there ought to be a law," pause. Ask what the law would actually do. Ask who would enforce it. Ask what happens when the enforcement fails. Then, and only then, decide if the law is the answer, or if it’s just the easiest place to put your frustration.

prompt: Everyone says 'there ought to be a law.' I'd like an essay arguing that most of the time there ought not to be, and that the impulse itself is worth examining. Not a libertarian rant please - more like, what are we really asking for when we say that?
response:
When a stranger cuts in line, a neighbor leaves their trash cans out for a week, or a friend cancels plans at the last minute, the reflex is immediate and uniform: *there ought to be a law.*

This is not a proposal. It is a sigh. It is a way of externalizing frustration. When we say a thing "ought to be" illegal, we are not usually calling for legislation. We are calling for a third party to enforce our preference. We want the world to have the consistency of a machine, where inputs produce predictable outputs, and where no one can deviate from the script without being stopped by a hand in a uniform.

The impulse reveals a specific anxiety about social order. We often mistake etiquette for morality, and we mistake morality for law. But the law is not a moral compass; it is a blunt instrument designed for violence. It is the last resort, the thing we do when persuasion, reputation, and mutual benefit have failed. To apply it to minor irritations is to treat a papercut with a chainsaw.

Consider the cost. A law is not just a rule; it is an infrastructure. It requires drafting, debate, enactment, enforcement, adjudication, and appeal. It creates a class of enforcers and a class of offenders. It shifts the power dynamic from horizontal—neighbor to neighbor—to vertical—citizen to state. When we demand a law for a trivial infraction, we are asking to replace a conversation with a complaint. We are asking the government to become a mediator in every petty dispute, which is an impossible job and an intrusive one.

There is also the danger of the slippery slope of specificity. If we can pass a law against loud dogs, we must define "loud." If we define "loud," we must define the time of day. If we define the time of day, we must define who is allowed to make noise. The code of conduct for daily life becomes a manual that no one has read and everyone violates. The result is not order, but a web of technicalities where the only winners are the lawyers and the bureaucrats who profit from the complexity.

The true function of law is to protect us from harm that we cannot protect against ourselves. It stops the thief, the murderer, the contract breaker. It exists because there are things that individuals, acting alone, cannot do. You cannot punch a burglar if he is not in your house. You cannot sue a stranger in a different state. The law bridges the gap between private capacity and public safety.

When we expand the law to cover things we *can* handle ourselves—things that involve social pressure, guilt, or simple avoidance—we dilute its authority. If the police are called for a dispute over a hedge or a noise complaint, they are not protecting the peace; they are managing the annoyance. And in doing so, they train us to view the state as the default arbiter of all human interaction. We stop asking, "Can I live with this?" and start asking, "Can I make them stop?"

The impulse to legislate the minor is a failure of imagination. It assumes that the only solution to a problem is the cessation of the problem. It ignores the messy, inefficient, human reality of living in close proximity to other people who have different tastes, schedules, and priorities.

We do not need a law against rudeness. We need the social capital to tolerate it, or the distance to avoid it. We do not need a law against bad taste. We need the market to punish it. We do not need a law against selfishness. We need the community to ostracize it.

The law is sacred precisely because it is rare. Its weight comes from its restraint. When we ask for a law for everything, we do not get a better society. We get a smaller one, where every action is watched, every preference is policed, and every interaction is a potential violation. We want the world to be safe, which is fair. But we also want it to be free, which requires letting the minor things stand.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay that the US should pay jurors a real wage - currently many states pay $15-50 a day - and what the low pay does to who ends up on juries.
response:
The American jury system was designed to be a check on government power, composed of ordinary citizens who bring a "common sense" perspective to the law. That design assumes that anyone can afford to stop what they are doing to sit in a courtroom for three days or three months. In reality, the daily per diem of $15 to $50 in most states makes that impossible for the working poor. The result is a jury pool that is disproportionately white, older, and wealthy, while the people who are most likely to be tried by a jury—low-income defendants of color—are excluded from the process that decides their fate.

The math is simple. A day’s pay of $25 does not cover a day’s living expenses. It does not cover childcare, which costs more than the daily stipend in most urban areas. It does not cover the transportation to get to the courthouse, nor the lost wages for the remainder of the week if the trial drags on. For a salaried employee, the employer might cover the difference, but only if the company can afford to lose a worker for an indeterminate period. For a hourly worker, the check simply does not arrive. They are told to pick a different week, or they are fired.

This creates a structural bias in who serves. The people who can afford to be jurors are those who have financial buffers: retirees, freelancers with flexible schedules, or employees at companies that value their presence enough to make up the difference. The people who cannot are those with the least job security. They are the ones most likely to be in the defendant’s chair. When a jury is composed entirely of people who have never worried about making rent, their understanding of desperation is theoretical. They may view a charge of shoplifting or possession as a moral failing rather than a symptom of economic precarity. They may view a delay in court as an inconvenience rather than a financial catastrophe.

Critics argue that paying jurors a full market wage would be too expensive or would encourage people to serve as a form of employment. The cost argument is weak when weighed against the cost of a biased system. The federal government already pays jurors $60 a day, and many states have moved to higher rates, yet the gap remains. To make the system fair, the pay must reflect the actual cost of absence. That means paying minimum wage for the hours served, plus benefits, or providing a stipend that covers lost income.

A jury that reflects the demographic and economic reality of the community is not just a matter of representation; it is a matter of legitimacy. If the community cannot be in the box, the verdict is not the community’s judgment. It is the judgment of a specific class of people with the luxury of time. Until the pay reflects the reality of work, the jury box will remain a place where the poor are judged by the rich, and the system will fail its most basic promise of equality.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay that the US should pay jurors a real wage - currently many states pay $15-50 a day - and what the low pay does to who ends up on juries.
response:
The American jury system is not a market. It is a civic obligation enforced by the state, yet the compensation for fulfilling that obligation is often below the federal minimum wage. In many states, jurors are paid between $15 and $50 a day. For a week-long trial, that amounts to less than the cost of a week’s groceries. This pay structure does not reflect the value of the work; it reflects a historical assumption that justice is a privilege only the wealthy can afford to give.

The result is a demographic skew that undermines the jury’s primary function: to represent the community. When service requires a sacrifice of income, the pool of eligible citizens shrinks. People who can easily take a week off without financial ruin—retirees, stay-at-home parents, freelancers, and the very wealthy—are overrepresented. People who cannot—teachers, nurses, retail workers, and hourly laborers—are underrepresented. The jury box becomes a sample of the leisure class rather than a cross-section of the population.

This distortion matters because jurors are not just fact-finders; they are the conscience of the community. They bring their lived experiences, their understanding of cost and consequence, and their instincts about fairness to the table. A jury composed primarily of people who have never worried about whether they can afford to eat this week does not weigh the same evidence the same way as one that includes them. When a defendant argues that his poverty drove him to theft, or when a plaintiff argues that the injury has bankrupted her family, the empathy required to understand those claims is filtered through the jurors’ own economic security. If the state wants a jury of peers, it must make service accessible to the actual peer group: the working class.

Critics argue that high wages would attract professional jurors, people who would serve to earn a living rather than to do a civic duty. This is a false dichotomy. The current system already attracts a different kind of professional: those who have the luxury of time. We do not fear that high school teachers will stop teaching to sit on juries; we fear that they will be fired or fined for missing work. Paying a real wage—say, $150 a day, aligned with the average hourly wage of a full-time worker—does not create a class of professional jurors. It eliminates the penalty for doing one’s duty.

The state demands that citizens risk their freedom by sitting in judgment on their neighbors. It demands their time, their attention, and their mental energy. In return, it offers a token amount of money and a pat on the back. If the government wants the participation of the people it governs, it must treat that participation as work, not as a hobby. Until it does, the jury will remain a body of the few, judging the many.

prompt: An essay on the pardon power: why do democracies keep a relic of monarchical mercy, and what would we lose if we abolished it?
response:
The pardon is a strange survival. In a constitutional democracy, the executive branch is supposed to enforce the law, not suspend it. Yet in the United States, the President can unilaterally erase a conviction for any federal crime, with no judicial review, no legislative oversight, and no requirement to explain the decision. It is the last vestige of the sovereign’s absolute will, transplanted into a republic that claims all power resides in the people.

We keep it because we fear the law is sometimes cruel, and we do not trust the courts to fix it.

The legal system is rigid. Judges interpret statutes; they cannot rewrite them mid-sentence. When a law is just in principle but produces an absurd or unjust result in a specific case, the judicial system has no mechanism to step back and say, “This is wrong.” The judge must follow the letter of the law. The jury may show mercy through a partial verdict, but that is an act of rebellion, not a sanctioned correction. The pardon is the only official channel for moral correction within the legal apparatus. It acknowledges that legal correctness and moral justice are not always the same thing.

Without it, we lose the ability to repair our mistakes. History is full of laws that seemed reasonable at the time but were later recognized as oppressive. The pardon allows a society to correct its course without repealing the law for everyone. It lets the state say, “We were wrong about this specific person, or this specific application,” while maintaining the general rule. If we abolished the pardon, the only recourse for a wrongly convicted or excessively punished citizen would be legislative repeal, which is slow, political, and retroactive in a way that invites legislative overreach.

Critics argue that the power is inherently corrupt. They point to the "pardon broker" scandals, where presidents or their aides have traded clemency for money or political loyalty. They are right that the power invites abuse. A pardon granted for cash is a sale of justice. A pardon granted to protect a friend is nepotism. But the alternative is not a cleaner system; it is a stiffer one. If the power is too dangerous to grant to one person, the answer is not to remove it, but to constrain it.

Other democracies have tried. The United Kingdom abolished the royal prerogative of mercy in the 1990s, replacing it with a statutory commutation scheme. The result was not a purer justice system but a more bureaucratic one. The power to mitigate a sentence now rests with judges, who are bound by sentencing guidelines. When a case clearly calls for leniency—perhaps due to a defendant’s mental state, age, or the futility of the punishment—the judge’s hands are often tied by the framework of their own authority. The UK system removed the scandal of the broker, but it also removed the voice of the sovereign conscience. It made mercy a legal calculation rather than a moral judgment.

The danger of the American pardon is that it is unchecked. But the danger of abolishing it is that we make the law a machine that cannot bend. We lose the recognition that justice is a human endeavor, subject to error, bias, and the slow dawning of moral understanding.

We should not keep the pardon because it is a relic of kings. We should keep it because we are not kings, and we know we are wrong. The power to forgive is the power to admit that the code we wrote does not fully capture the world we live in. Abolishing it would be an act of arrogance, a declaration that our statutes are perfect and our judges infallible. We are neither.

prompt: An essay on the pardon power: why do democracies keep a relic of monarchical mercy, and what would we lose if we abolished it?
response:
The pardon power is often described as a check on judicial error, a safety valve for systemic injustice, or a mechanism for national reconciliation. These are the justifications offered in textbooks and legislative hearings. They are not why the power exists.

The pardon is a survival strategy for the state. It allows the executive to absorb the political cost of a bad law, a corrupt prosecutor, or a judge who overreached, without admitting that the legal system itself is broken. In a monarchy, mercy was the sole proof that the king’s justice was not merely the imposition of his will, but the administration of a higher moral order. The king punished; the king forgave. The cycle was complete, and the authority remained intact.

In a democracy, the cycle is broken. The judge is an independent actor, not an arm of the executive. When the judiciary renders a verdict that the public or the president finds unjust, the executive cannot simply overrule it without violating separation of powers. The pardon bridges this gap. It allows the executive to say, “The law was applied correctly, but the outcome was wrong, and I, as the representative of the people, correct it.”

This is not a relic. It is a necessary friction. Without it, the law becomes a machine that runs past the point of moral viability. Consider the case of the soldier who follows an unlawful order, or the whistleblower who leaks a secret to prevent a greater harm. The statute book has no category for their specific nuance. The jury might convict on the letter of the law, but the public knows the truth. If the executive cannot intervene, the state is forced to either let an injustice stand or repeal the statute entirely. Repealing the statute changes the law for everyone; pardoning the individual isolates the mercy. The latter preserves the general rule while acknowledging its failure in a specific instance.

What would be lost in abolition? The primary loss is the executive’s ability to manage the narrative of justice. The pardon is a tool of political stabilization. It allows a president to grant clemency to a controversial figure, thereby diffusing the anger of that figure’s supporters without capitulating to their demands on the merits. It is a way to buy time. It says, “We see your grievance, we do not agree with the law as written, but we will not tear down the institution to fix this one case.”

Critics argue this makes the pardon a tool of partisan reward. They are right. Presidents have pardoned allies for crimes and rivals for crimes. The power is inherently subjective because justice, at the margins, is inherently subjective. But a system that eliminates subjective mercy to prevent subjective corruption ends up with a system that is only as good as its worst statute.

There is a deeper danger in abolishing the pardon: it hardens the distinction between the legal and the political. Currently, the pardon forces the executive to engage with the judiciary’s output in a public, reasoned way. A pardon is a statement. It says, “This verdict was legally sound but morally wrong.” If that statement can no longer be made by the chief executive, the disagreement between the branches goes underground. It becomes a quiet tension, a refusal to cooperate, a subtle obstruction. The pardon forces the conflict into the open, where it can be debated, criticized, and, eventually, resolved through legislation or constitutional amendment.

Abolishing the power would not make the law more just. It would make the law more rigid. It would remove the one mechanism by which the state can acknowledge that its own rules have failed, without admitting that the rules themselves are invalid. The democracy keeps the relic because it needs the excuse. It needs the ability to say that the system worked, even when the result was a disaster.

prompt: I work in procurement for a city government. Every scandal leads to a new rule, every rule adds paperwork, and now buying a $400 printer takes six weeks. I want an essay about the ratchet effect of anti-corruption rules, written for a smart non-specialist reader. Fair to both sides - corruption is real.
response:
The printer sits in a box in the supply closet. It is a $400 laser jet. It has been waiting for six weeks for three signatures, a competitive bid analysis, and a file folder that must be indexed correctly. The person who needs it is typing on a ten-year-old machine with a stuck 'e' key.

This is not a joke. It is the result of a feedback loop that has captured most large bureaucracies, from city halls to federal agencies. The loop is simple: corruption occurs, the public panics, legislators pass a law, the law creates a procedure, the procedure creates a cost, and the cost creates a new incentive to cheat.

### The Ratchet

In engineering, a ratchet is a mechanism that allows motion in only one direction. Anti-corruption policy behaves the same way. When a scandal breaks—say, a city councilman takes a kickback from a paving contractor—the political response is immediate and visceral. The public does not want a nuanced study on procurement incentives. They want the bad guy in jail and a rule that makes it impossible for the next bad guy to do the same thing.

So the rule is passed. Perhaps it requires that any purchase over $5,000 must be competitively bid by at least three vendors. This is a reasonable idea in the abstract. In practice, it transforms a transaction into a legal proceeding.

The first effect of the rule is compliance cost. The procurement officer must now solicit bids, track responses, evaluate them against a matrix of criteria, and document why the winning bid was selected. This takes time. It takes paper. It takes attention.

The second effect is more subtle: it changes who is in the room. The people best equipped to navigate a complex, document-heavy process are not the engineers who know what the city actually needs. They are the lawyers, the lobbyists, and the large vendors with dedicated government-relations teams. The small, nimble supplier who could have delivered the printer in two days is priced out because he cannot afford to fill out the bid forms. The large supplier, who can afford the compliance overhead, wins the contract at a premium. The city pays more for the same good.

The third effect is the most dangerous. When the cost of doing business legally exceeds the benefit, the incentive to cheat shifts. The procurement officer, under pressure to deliver goods within a tight budget and timeline, may find that the easiest way to stay within the rules is to manipulate the criteria. If the rule says "lowest responsive bid wins," but the low bidder is incompetent, the officer can tweak the evaluation matrix to disqualify them. Now the officer has committed a fraud, but it looks like a technicality.

### The Feedback Loop

This is the ratchet. The original rule was designed to stop the kickback. The new rule, by making honest compliance so expensive and slow, creates the conditions for the kickback to return in a new form.

Consider the printer. If the city had a system where a designated buyer could purchase low-value items with a credit card, subject to random audit, the printer would be in the box in two days. The risk of corruption exists, but it is manageable. The audit trail is clear. The cost of compliance is near zero.

Instead, the city has a system where the cost of compliance is so high that the system itself becomes the product. Vendors compete not on price or quality, but on their ability to produce the correct paperwork. Procurement officers compete not on value, but on their ability to survive an audit.

This is why the rules never stop coming. Every time a new loophole is found—because human beings are creative and incentives are strong—a new rule is added. The paper pile grows. The time to buy a printer increases. The distance between the need and the fulfillment widens.

### The Other Side

It is important to be clear: the corruption is real. It is not a myth invented by bureaucrats to justify their power. When a city overpays by 30% for a bridge, that money does not vanish. It is stolen from the taxpayers. It is stolen from the schools and the roads and the libraries. The public anger is justified. The demand for accountability is democratic and necessary.

The problem is not that we want to prevent corruption. The problem is that we have chosen the wrong tools. We have tried to solve a behavioral problem with procedural ones. We have assumed that if we make the process opaque enough, the corruption will stop. In reality, opacity is the friend of corruption. Transparency is its enemy.
